title: The idle show
hookLine: processions, plays, dogs fighting over bones: stay good-natured among it all (Meditations 7.3)

cards: Scroll your phone for one minute. A celebrity feud. A dog in a costume.
Two strangers furious about a sandwich. A man falling into a pool, on repeat. A political fight, a pie-eating contest, an ad.
Loud, ridiculous, and it never stops. It might seem like a new problem. Marcus Aurelius had no phone, but he had Rome, and in book seven he wrote down his own scroll of the absurd.

teach.b: In Meditations seven, three, Marcus piles it up: the empty business of a parade, plays on the stage, flocks of sheep and herds of cattle, men fencing with spears, a bone tossed to puppies, a crumb thrown into a fishpond, ants hauling their loads, frightened mice running around, puppets jerked on strings.
Amid all of it, he says, be good-humored, not proud. Not sneering, not superior: kindly present. That's harder than it sounds, because when the world looks silly, the easy move is contempt.
Marcus tells himself not to take it.

teach.h: WORTH WHAT YOU BUSY YOURSELF WITH.
teach.b: Then the sting at the end: a person is worth just as much as the things they busy themselves about. Spend your life chasing bones, and that's the size of your life. So the good humor isn't indifference.
He's watching what people care about, himself included, and what it makes them.

teach.h: KIND TO THE SCENE, CHOOSY INSIDE.
teach.b: Hold those two together: kindness toward the silly scene, without being swallowed by it.

You can laugh with the dog in the costume, let the sandwich fight go by, and stay friendly at the office party where everyone is jockeying for the boss's attention, while quietly deciding where your own attention goes.
Good-natured on the outside. Choosy on the inside.

how: Readers of Marcus often use 7.3 to stay friendly in noisy or petty settings, from office politics to social media, without sneering at people and without letting the noise decide what they care about.

games.q: you're at a party where everyone is jockeying for attention, and it's a little absurd. what does Marcus advise?
o: join in and chase the attention too.
stay good-humored, not proud, and keep your own attention for what matters.
games.why: Meditations 7.3: amid the idle show, be good-humored and not proud, while knowing a person is worth what they busy themselves about.

practice: Picture a silly scene from your week, a meeting that went in circles, a family argument about nothing, a feed full of noise, and let any eye-roll soften.
See the people in it as Marcus saw the puppies with their bone: a little absurd, and fully alive. Then ask, gently, what you want to spend your own attention on.

wordCard.voice: Puppets. One image in Marcus's list of life's busy absurdities: puppets jerked on strings, among parades, plays and fights. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: good-natured. Kindness toward the show, and your attention kept for what matters. See you tomorrow.
